title: Supreme Court Says Missouri Will Use Its Old Voting Map — For Now
summary:
Imagine if your classroom seating chart changed three times before a test. That's kind of what's happening in Missouri.

On Friday, the Supreme Court said Missouri can't use a new congressional map backed by President Donald Trump for the November elections. Instead, voters will use the same districts from 2022 and 2024.

Why does this matter? These districts decide who represents people in Congress. Republicans had hoped the new map would help them win an extra seat. Missouri currently has eight House districts, and Republicans hold six.

The legal fight has been messy. The new map was already used in the August primaries. Then the Missouri Supreme Court said a citizen petition meant the map needed voter approval first. A federal appeals court disagreed. Finally, the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in.

"At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos," the justices wrote.

Absentee voting started Tuesday. More than a million voters — nearly 1 in 4 in Missouri — had been shifted between districts, so some ballots looked different. That caused confusion.

At least 16 lawsuits have been filed over this map. The Supreme Court's decision ends this round, but the fight over redistricting — how voting lines are drawn — is still going on in many states.
why_it_matters: The voting districts decide who represents your community in Congress, and those leaders make rules that affect your school, your town and your family.

background_read: Missouri is a state in the middle of the United States, and it has eight seats in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Every ten years the country counts how many people live where, and then states redraw their voting districts — something called redistricting.

Congress is the part of the U.S. government that makes laws, and its members are elected from districts like these; the Supreme Court (the country's highest court, with nine justices) often settles fights over voting maps.
Article_Structure: WHO: The U.S. Supreme Court, Missouri voters and election officials, President Donald Trump, and lower courts.
WHAT: The Supreme Court ruled that Missouri must use its older 2022 and 2024 districts for November instead of a new Trump-backed map.
WHERE: Missouri, a state in the middle of the United States.
WHY: The new map could have given Republicans one extra House seat, but the justices said switching maps in the middle of an election would cause 'electoral chaos.'

perspectives.perspective: Republicans who backed the new map
perspectives.description: They hoped the new districts would help them win an extra seat in Congress, and they say the map fits where people live now.

perspectives.perspective: People who fought the new map
perspectives.description: They say voters should get to approve big changes to voting lines, and that switching maps late confused people whose ballots had already changed.
They focused on keeping the election calm, saying a last-minute change would 'usher in electoral chaos.'
